_link.title: I can draw and interpret free-body diagrams showing all forces acting on a body

toLevel2.question: A free-body diagram is used to analyse the forces acting on an object. Which one of the following best describes what a free-body diagram shows?
toLevel2.correct: All forces acting on a single object
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A free-body diagram isolates one object and represents all external forces acting on it as arrows.

distractors.answer: The velocity and acceleration of an object
distractors.explanation: Velocity and acceleration are kinematic quantities, not forces; free-body diagrams show forces only.

distractors.answer: The motion path of an object over time
distractors.explanation: A trajectory or path diagram shows motion; a free-body diagram shows forces at a single instant.

distractors.answer: All objects involved in a force interaction
distractors.explanation: A free-body diagram isolates a single object; it does not show all objects in the interaction.

toLevel2.question: A student draws a free-body diagram of a stationary box on a table. Which one of the following best describes what the length of a force arrow represents in the diagram?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Longer arrows indicate larger forces; the arrow length is proportional to the force magnitude.

distractors.answer: The direction of the force only
distractors.explanation: Direction is shown by the arrow's orientation, not its length; length represents magnitude.

distractors.answer: The duration of the applied force
distractors.explanation: Arrow length does not represent how long a force acts; it represents the strength of the force.

distractors.answer: The distance the object will move
distractors.explanation: Arrow length represents force magnitude, not displacement; these are different physical quantities.

toLevel2.question: A ball is held at rest near the surface of Earth and then released. Which one of the following correctly identifies the force that acts on every object near Earth's surface and must appear on every free-body diagram of such objects?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The gravitational force (mg) acts on all objects near Earth's surface and is always drawn vertically downward on a free-body diagram.

distractors.answer: The normal force exerted by a surface
distractors.explanation: The normal force only exists when an object is in contact with a surface; it does not act on a falling object.

distractors.answer: The friction force from contact
distractors.explanation: Friction requires contact with a surface and a tendency to slide; it is not always present.

distractors.answer: The applied force from a push
distractors.explanation: An applied force only exists when something is actively pushing or pulling the object.

toLevel2.question: A box of mass 5.0 kg rests on a horizontal surface. Which one of the following best describes the direction of the normal force exerted on the box by the surface?
toLevel2.correct: Perpendicular to the surface, directed upward
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The normal force always acts perpendicular to the contact surface, which for a horizontal surface is vertically upward.

distractors.answer: Parallel to the surface, directed forward
distractors.explanation: Forces parallel to the surface are friction forces, not normal forces.

distractors.answer: Vertically downward toward the ground
distractors.explanation: The normal force acts upward from the surface; the gravitational force acts downward.

distractors.answer: At an angle between horizontal and vertical
distractors.explanation: On a horizontal surface the normal force is purely vertical; it is only angled on an inclined surface.

toLevel2.question: A student is constructing a free-body diagram of a block on a table. Which one of the following correctly identifies where force arrows should originate in the diagram?
toLevel2.correct: From the centre of the object
toLevel2.correctExplanation: In a standard free-body diagram, all force arrows are drawn originating from the centre of the object or a dot representing it.

distractors.answer: From the surface the object rests on
distractors.explanation: Force arrows start from the object itself, not from external surfaces or surroundings.

distractors.answer: From the edge of the object directed outward
distractors.explanation: While contact forces act at the surface, in a free-body diagram they are conventionally drawn from the centre point.

distractors.answer: From an external reference point nearby
distractors.explanation: Free-body diagram arrows originate from the object being analysed, not from external reference points.

toLevel2.question: A student states: 'In a free-body diagram, forces are drawn as arrows originating from the object, with arrow length proportional to force magnitude.' The student's statement is correct.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: This is the standard convention for free-body diagrams: arrows represent forces, and their length indicates relative magnitude.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: Proportional arrow length is the correct convention for representing force magnitude in free-body diagrams.

toLevel2.question: A student claims: 'A free-body diagram should show forces acting on all objects involved in a situation.' The student's claim is correct.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A free-body diagram isolates a single object and shows only the forces acting on that one object, not all objects in the scenario.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: A free-body diagram focuses on one object only; separate diagrams are drawn for each object in the interaction.

toLevel2.prompt: Complete the following description of a free-body diagram.
toLevel2.sentence: A free-body diagram shows the relative magnitude and {{blank:1}} of all forces acting on a {{blank:2}} object.

1.correctExplanation: Force arrows in a free-body diagram show both the magnitude (arrow length) and direction (arrow orientation) of each force.

distractors.answer: velocity
distractors.explanation: Velocity is a kinematic quantity, not a property of force arrows in a free-body diagram.

distractors.answer: duration
distractors.explanation: Duration refers to how long a force acts; free-body diagrams show magnitude and direction, not time.

2.correctExplanation: A free-body diagram isolates one object and shows only the forces on that single object.

distractors.answer: moving
distractors.explanation: Free-body diagrams can be drawn for stationary or moving objects; the key feature is isolating a single object.

distractors.answer: massive
distractors.explanation: Free-body diagrams can be drawn for any object regardless of mass; they isolate a single object.

toLevel2.prompt: A box sits on a horizontal table with no other forces acting. Complete the following description of the forces in its free-body diagram.
toLevel2.sentence: The free-body diagram includes the {{blank:1}} acting downward and the {{blank:2}} acting upward.

1.correctExplanation: The gravitational force (mg) always acts vertically downward on objects near Earth's surface.

distractors.answer: normal force
distractors.explanation: The normal force acts upward from the surface, not downward; the gravitational force is the downward force.

distractors.answer: friction force
distractors.explanation: Friction acts parallel to the surface; the downward force on the box is the gravitational force.

2.correctExplanation: The normal force is the contact force exerted on the box by the table surface, acting perpendicular (upward) to the horizontal surface.

distractors.answer: applied force
distractors.explanation: An applied force only exists if something is pushing or pulling the box; the upward contact force from the table is the normal force.

distractors.answer: tension force
distractors.explanation: Tension acts through strings or ropes; the upward force exerted on the box by the table surface is the normal force.

toLevel2.prompt: A block rests on an inclined surface. Complete the following description of the forces in its free-body diagram.
toLevel2.sentence: For an object on a slope, the normal force acts {{blank:1}} to the slope surface, while the gravitational force acts vertically {{blank:2}}.

1.correctExplanation: The normal force always acts at right angles (perpendicular) to the contact surface, including on inclined planes.

distractors.answer: parallel
distractors.explanation: Forces parallel to the slope are friction or components of the gravitational force, not the normal force.

distractors.answer: opposite
distractors.explanation: 'Opposite' does not describe a geometric relationship to the surface; the normal force is specifically perpendicular to the surface.

2.correctExplanation: The gravitational force always acts vertically downward toward the centre of Earth, regardless of the orientation of the surface.

distractors.answer: along the slope
distractors.explanation: A component of the gravitational force acts along the slope, but the gravitational force itself acts vertically downward.

distractors.answer: perpendicular to the slope
distractors.explanation: A component of the gravitational force acts perpendicular to the slope, but the full gravitational force vector acts vertically downward.

toLevel3.question: A block of mass 4.0 kg is at rest on a rough inclined plane. A student draws a free-body diagram showing friction directed up the slope. Which one of the following best explains why friction acts up the slope?
toLevel3.correct: Friction opposes the tendency of the block to slide down the slope
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Static friction acts in the direction that prevents motion; since the gravitational force pulls the block down the slope, friction acts up the slope.

distractors.answer: Friction always acts in the same direction as the normal force
distractors.explanation: Friction acts parallel to the surface, while the normal force acts perpendicular; they are in different directions.

distractors.answer: Friction acts up the slope to push the block toward the top
distractors.explanation: Friction does not push the block up; it prevents the block from sliding down. It acts to oppose the tendency of motion.

distractors.answer: Friction acts in the direction of the gravitational force component along the slope
distractors.explanation: Friction opposes the tendency of motion; the gravitational force component along the slope pulls the block down, so friction acts up.

toLevel3.question: A block of mass 6.0 kg sits on an inclined plane at 25° to the horizontal. A student claims that the normal force exerted on the block by the surface equals the gravitational force on the block. Which one of the following best explains why this claim is incorrect?
toLevel3.correct: The normal force only balances the component of the gravitational force perpendicular to the slope
toLevel3.correctExplanation: On a slope, the gravitational force has components both parallel and perpendicular to the surface. The normal force equals only the perpendicular component.

distractors.answer: The normal force is reduced by friction acting along the slope surface
distractors.explanation: Friction acts parallel to the slope and does not affect the perpendicular normal force.

distractors.answer: The normal force is always less than the gravitational force for any object on a surface
distractors.explanation: On a horizontal surface, the normal force equals the gravitational force; it is only on an incline that it is less.

distractors.answer: The incline absorbs some of the gravitational force acting on the block
distractors.explanation: The gravitational force is not absorbed; it is resolved into two components, and the normal force balances only the perpendicular one.

toLevel3.question: A lamp of mass 2.5 kg hangs from a single cord attached to the ceiling. The lamp is stationary. A student draws a free-body diagram showing the gravitational force downward and tension upward. Which one of the following best describes the relationship between these two forces?
toLevel3.correct: The tension and the gravitational force are equal in magnitude, and the net force is zero
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Since the lamp is stationary (zero acceleration), the upward tension must equal the downward gravitational force for the forces to be balanced.

distractors.answer: The tension is greater than the gravitational force because the lamp hangs above the ground
distractors.explanation: If tension exceeded the gravitational force there would be a net upward force and the lamp would accelerate upward.

distractors.answer: The gravitational force is greater than the tension because gravity is the dominant force
distractors.explanation: For a stationary object the forces must balance; the relative dominance of gravity is irrelevant here.

distractors.answer: The two forces cancel each other completely, meaning no forces act on the lamp
distractors.explanation: The forces balance to produce zero net force, but both forces still act on the lamp; they are not eliminated.

toLevel3.question: A ball is thrown into the air. Ignore air resistance. At a point during the ball's flight, a student draws its free-body diagram. Which one of the following correctly identifies the number of forces that should appear on the diagram?
toLevel3.correct: One force: the gravitational force acting downward
toLevel3.correctExplanation: In mid-air with no air resistance, the only force acting on the ball is the gravitational force, acting vertically downward.

distractors.answer: Two forces: the gravitational force downward and a forward throwing force
distractors.explanation: Once the ball leaves the hand, the throwing force no longer acts; only the gravitational force remains.

distractors.answer: Three forces: the gravitational force, the normal force, and air resistance
distractors.explanation: There is no surface contact for a normal force and air resistance is ignored; only the gravitational force acts.

distractors.answer: Zero forces, because the ball is in free flight
distractors.explanation: The gravitational force still acts on the ball in flight; free flight does not mean force-free.

toLevel3.question: A student is drawing a free-body diagram of a crate on a factory floor. Which one of the following best explains why it is important that force arrows have lengths proportional to the magnitudes of the forces?
toLevel3.correct: It allows visual identification of whether forces are balanced or unbalanced
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Proportional arrows make it easy to see which forces are larger, whether forces balance, and the likely direction of the net force.

distractors.answer: It shows the exact numerical value of each force acting on the object
distractors.explanation: Proportional arrows show relative magnitude, not exact values; numerical labels provide exact values.

distractors.answer: It determines the direction of motion of the object being analysed
distractors.explanation: Direction of motion is not directly shown by force arrow lengths; arrow direction and magnitude show net force direction.

distractors.answer: It is a purely cosmetic convention with no analytical significance
distractors.explanation: Proportional arrows provide important analytical information about force balance and net force direction.

toLevel3.question: An object of mass 8.0 kg is pulled across a rough horizontal surface by a horizontal rope. Which one of the following correctly identifies all the forces that should appear on the free-body diagram?
toLevel3.correct: The gravitational force, the normal force, the tension in the rope, and friction
toLevel3.correctExplanation: All four forces act: the gravitational force downward, the normal force upward, tension forward from the rope, and friction backward opposing motion.

distractors.answer: The gravitational force, the normal force, and the tension in the rope only
distractors.explanation: Friction must be included because the surface is rough and the object is moving along it.

distractors.answer: The gravitational force, tension, friction, and an acceleration force
distractors.explanation: Acceleration is not a force; it is the result of a net force. Only real forces appear on free-body diagrams.

distractors.answer: Tension and friction only, since they cause horizontal motion
distractors.explanation: The gravitational force and the normal force must also be included; they act vertically and are essential for a complete diagram.

toLevel3.question: A student claims: 'The normal force exerted on an object resting on an inclined plane is equal to the gravitational force on the object.' The student's claim is correct.
toLevel3.correctExplanation: On an incline, the normal force equals only the component of the gravitational force perpendicular to the surface (mg cos θ), which is less than the full gravitational force.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: This is only true on a horizontal surface. On an incline, the gravitational force has a component along the slope, so the normal force is less than the gravitational force.

toLevel3.prompt: A block rests on an inclined plane. Complete the following explanation about the forces in the free-body diagram.
toLevel3.sentence: On an inclined plane, the gravitational force on the object is resolved into a component {{blank:1}} to the slope and a component perpendicular to the slope. The component along the slope tends to cause the object to {{blank:2}} the slope.

1.correctExplanation: The gravitational force is resolved into two components: one parallel to the slope surface and one perpendicular to it.

distractors.answer: opposite
distractors.explanation: 'Opposite' does not describe a geometric relationship to the surface; the component is parallel to the slope.

distractors.answer: tangential
distractors.explanation: While tangential can mean parallel in some contexts, in VCE physics the standard term is 'parallel to the slope'.

2.correctExplanation: The component of the gravitational force parallel to the slope acts down the slope, tending to pull the object toward the bottom.

distractors.answer: push away from
distractors.explanation: The gravitational force component along the slope pulls the object down the slope, not away from the surface.

distractors.answer: lift off
distractors.explanation: No component of the gravitational force acts upward; both components act downward relative to the slope and vertically.

toLevel3.prompt: A lamp hangs from a single cord attached to the ceiling and is stationary. Complete the following description of the free-body diagram.
toLevel3.sentence: The free-body diagram shows {{blank:1}} acting upward along the cord and the {{blank:2}} acting vertically downward.

1.correctExplanation: The cord exerts an upward tension force on the lamp, supporting it against the gravitational force.

distractors.answer: normal force
distractors.explanation: The normal force requires contact with a surface; the upward force from a cord is tension.

distractors.answer: applied force
distractors.explanation: The force exerted on the lamp by a cord is specifically called tension, not a general applied force.

2.correctExplanation: The gravitational force acts vertically downward on the lamp.

distractors.answer: friction force
distractors.explanation: Friction requires contact with a surface and relative motion; there is no friction on a hanging lamp.

distractors.answer: drag force
distractors.explanation: Drag requires motion through a fluid; a stationary hanging lamp has no drag force.

toLevel3.prompt: Complete the following explanation about the role of free-body diagrams in solving force problems.
toLevel3.sentence: Free-body diagrams are essential because they allow identification of all forces, determination of the {{blank:1}}, and application of Newton's {{blank:2}} law to solve for acceleration.

1.correctExplanation: By showing all forces, a free-body diagram allows the forces to be summed vectorially to find the net (resultant) force.

distractors.answer: total mass
distractors.explanation: Free-body diagrams display forces, not masses; mass is a separate quantity used in Fnet = ma.

distractors.answer: contact area
distractors.explanation: Contact area is not determined from a free-body diagram; the diagram shows force vectors.

2.correctExplanation: Once the net force is known from the diagram, Newton's second law (Fnet = ma) is applied to find acceleration.

distractors.answer: first
distractors.explanation: Newton's first law describes equilibrium conditions; the second law is used to calculate acceleration from net force.

distractors.answer: third
distractors.explanation: Newton's third law identifies action-reaction pairs; the second law relates net force to acceleration.

toLevel4.question: A block of mass 5.0 kg is placed on a frictionless ramp inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Which one of the following correctly identifies the forces on the free-body diagram and the net force acting on the block?
toLevel4.correct: The gravitational force (49 N downward) and the normal force perpendicular to the ramp; the net force is 24.5 N directed down the slope
toLevel4.correctExplanation: The gravitational force is mg = 49 N. The component along the slope is mg sin 30° = 24.5 N. With no friction, this is the net force down the slope.

distractors.answer: The gravitational force (49 N downward) and the normal force perpendicular to the ramp; the net force is 42.4 N directed down the slope
distractors.explanation: 42.4 N = mg cos 30°, which is the perpendicular component balanced by the normal force, not the net force along the slope.

distractors.answer: The gravitational force (49 N downward) and friction up the slope; the net force is zero because the block is stationary
distractors.explanation: The ramp is frictionless; without friction, the block accelerates down the slope with a net force of mg sin 30°.

distractors.answer: The gravitational force (49 N downward) only, with no normal force; the net force is 49 N directed vertically downward
distractors.explanation: The ramp exerts a normal force perpendicular to its surface; without it the block would fall through the ramp.

toLevel4.question: A crate of mass 10 kg is pushed across a rough horizontal floor by a horizontal force of 60 N. The friction force acting on the crate is 40 N. Which one of the following correctly describes the free-body diagram of the crate?
toLevel4.correct: Gravitational force 98 N downward, normal force 98 N upward, 60 N applied force forward, 40 N friction backward
toLevel4.correctExplanation: All four forces are present: the gravitational force and normal force balance vertically (98 N each), the applied force and friction act horizontally with a net force of 20 N forward.

distractors.answer: Gravitational force 98 N downward, normal force 98 N upward, 20 N net force forward only
distractors.explanation: Free-body diagrams show individual forces, not just the net force; all four separate forces must appear.

distractors.answer: Gravitational force 98 N downward, normal force 58 N upward, 60 N applied force forward, 40 N friction backward
distractors.explanation: The normal force equals the gravitational force for a horizontal surface with a horizontal push; 58 N incorrectly subtracts friction from the normal force.

distractors.answer: Gravitational force 98 N downward, normal force 98 N upward, 60 N applied force forward, no friction since the crate is moving
distractors.explanation: Kinetic friction acts on the crate while it slides; friction does not disappear during motion.

toLevel4.question: A student draws a free-body diagram for a ball thrown vertically upward that is currently moving upward. Ignore air resistance. The student includes the gravitational force downward and an 'upward force from the throw'. Which one of the following best describes the correction needed?
toLevel4.correct: Remove the upward throw force; only the gravitational force acts on the ball in flight
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Once the ball leaves the hand, the throwing force no longer acts. In flight (ignoring air resistance), the gravitational force is the only force.

distractors.answer: Keep the upward force but make it smaller than the gravitational force to show deceleration
distractors.explanation: No upward force exists after release; deceleration is caused by the gravitational force alone, not by a reduced upward force.

distractors.answer: Add an air resistance force directed downward to replace the throw force
distractors.explanation: Air resistance acts opposite to motion (downward for an upward-moving ball would be incorrect) and the question states to ignore air resistance.

distractors.answer: Add a normal force directed downward since the ball was recently in contact with the hand
distractors.explanation: The normal force requires current contact; once the ball is released there is no normal force from the hand.

toLevel4.question: A mass of 2.0 kg hangs from two ropes that make different angles with the ceiling. The mass is stationary. Which one of the following correctly identifies the number of force arrows that should appear on the free-body diagram of the mass?
toLevel4.correct: Three: the gravitational force downward and two tension forces, one along each rope
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Each rope exerts a separate tension force on the mass, and the gravitational force acts downward, giving three forces total.

distractors.answer: Two: the gravitational force downward and a single combined tension force upward
distractors.explanation: Each rope has its own tension; they should be drawn separately, not combined into one arrow.

distractors.answer: Four: the gravitational force, two tensions, and a normal force from the ropes
distractors.explanation: Ropes exert tension, not normal forces; there are only three forces on the hanging mass.

distractors.answer: One: only the gravitational force, because the ropes simply hold the mass in position
distractors.explanation: The tension forces exerted on the mass by the ropes are real forces that must appear on the free-body diagram.

toLevel4.question: A car travels around a level circular track at constant speed. Which one of the following best describes the horizontal force shown on the free-body diagram of the car?
toLevel4.correct: A friction force directed toward the centre of the circular track
toLevel4.correctExplanation: On a level track, static friction between the tyres and the road provides the centripetal force, directed inward toward the centre.

distractors.answer: A centrifugal force directed outward from the centre of the track
distractors.explanation: In an inertial reference frame there is no centrifugal force; the real force is friction acting inward.

distractors.answer: No horizontal forces, because the car moves at constant speed
distractors.explanation: Constant speed with changing direction requires a centripetal force; friction provides this force horizontally.

distractors.answer: A forward driving force balanced by friction in the backward direction
distractors.explanation: The friction providing the centripetal force is directed radially inward, not backward along the track.

toLevel4.question: A block of mass 3.0 kg sits on a rough incline at 30° to the horizontal. The block is stationary. The component of the gravitational force along the slope is 14.7 N. Which one of the following best describes the friction force acting on the block?
toLevel4.correct: Static friction is 14.7 N directed up the slope, preventing the block from sliding
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Since the block is stationary, friction must exactly balance the gravitational force component along the slope (14.7 N) to give zero net force along the slope.

distractors.answer: Kinetic friction is 14.7 N directed down the slope, opposing motion
distractors.explanation: The block is stationary, so static friction (not kinetic) acts, and it acts up the slope to prevent sliding down.

distractors.answer: Static friction is greater than 14.7 N to hold the block firmly in place
distractors.explanation: Friction equals exactly 14.7 N for equilibrium; if it were greater, the block would accelerate up the slope.

distractors.answer: Friction is zero because the block is not moving
distractors.explanation: Static friction acts even when an object is stationary, preventing the block from sliding down the slope.

toLevel4.question: An object of mass 5.0 kg is dragged along a horizontal surface by a rope angled at 25° above the horizontal. Compared to a horizontal pull, which one of the following best describes how the angled pull affects the normal force exerted on the object by the surface?
toLevel4.correct: The normal force is reduced because the vertical component of the tension supports part of the gravitational force
toLevel4.correctExplanation: The upward component of the angled tension (T sin 25°) partially supports the gravitational force, so the surface provides a smaller normal force.

distractors.answer: The normal force increases because the pull adds a downward vertical component
distractors.explanation: A pull above horizontal has an upward vertical component, reducing the normal force, not increasing it.

distractors.answer: The normal force remains the same regardless of the angle of the pull
distractors.explanation: The vertical component of the pull changes the balance of vertical forces, altering the normal force.

distractors.answer: The normal force becomes zero because the rope lifts the object off the surface
distractors.explanation: The normal force is reduced but not zero unless the vertical tension component equals the gravitational force.

toLevel4.prompt: A block sits on a frictionless ramp inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Complete the following analysis of the gravitational force components.
toLevel4.sentence: The component of the gravitational force along the slope is mg {{blank:1}} 30° and the component perpendicular to the slope is mg {{blank:2}} 30°.

1.correctExplanation: The component of the gravitational force parallel (along) the slope is mg sin θ, where θ is the angle of inclination.

distractors.answer: cos
distractors.explanation: mg cos θ gives the component perpendicular to the slope, not along it.

distractors.answer: tan
distractors.explanation: Tangent is not used to resolve the gravitational force into slope components; sine and cosine are the correct functions.

2.correctExplanation: The component of the gravitational force perpendicular to the slope is mg cos θ, and this is balanced by the normal force.

distractors.answer: sin
distractors.explanation: mg sin θ gives the component parallel to the slope, not perpendicular to it.

distractors.answer: tan
distractors.explanation: Tangent is not used for resolving the gravitational force into components on an incline; cosine gives the perpendicular component.

toLevel4.prompt: An object of mass 4.0 kg hangs from a single vertical string and is stationary. Complete the following analysis of the free-body diagram.
toLevel4.sentence: The gravitational force on the object is {{blank:1}} N, so the tension in the string must be {{blank:2}} N for the object to remain at rest.

1.correctExplanation: Gravitational force = mg = 4.0 × 9.8 = 39.2 N acting downward.

distractors.explanation: This uses g = 10 m s⁻² instead of 9.8 m s⁻²; the correct value with g = 9.8 m s⁻² is 39.2 N.
19.6 N = 2.0 × 9.8, which uses the wrong mass; the object has a mass of 4.0 kg, giving 39.2 N.

2.correctExplanation: For the object to be at rest, the net force is zero, so tension must equal the gravitational force: 39.2 N upward.

distractors.explanation: 78.4 N is double the gravitational force; tension equals the gravitational force for a stationary hanging object, not double.
19.6 N is half the gravitational force; if tension were less than the gravitational force the object would accelerate downward.

toLevel4.prompt: A box is pushed with a horizontal force of 100 N across a rough floor. The friction force is 70 N. Complete the following analysis of the free-body diagram.
toLevel4.sentence: The net horizontal force is {{blank:1}} N forward, so the box is {{blank:2}}.

1.correctExplanation: Net force = applied force − friction = 100 − 70 = 30 N in the forward direction.

distractors.explanation: 170 N adds the force magnitudes instead of subtracting; since they oppose each other, the net force is their difference.
100 N is the applied force alone; friction must be subtracted to find the net force.

2.correctExplanation: A non-zero net force means the box has a non-zero acceleration in the forward direction.

distractors.answer: decelerating
distractors.explanation: The net force is forward (same direction as motion), so the box accelerates, not decelerates.

distractors.answer: at constant velocity
distractors.explanation: Constant velocity requires zero net force; a 30 N net force means the box accelerates.

toLevel5.question: A student draws a free-body diagram of a book resting on a table. The diagram shows the gravitational force, the normal force, and a separate arrow labelled 'the force of the table holding the book up'. Which one of the following best evaluates this diagram?
toLevel5.correct: The diagram has an error: the normal force is the force exerted on the book by the table, so it has been counted twice
toLevel5.correctExplanation: The normal force exerted on the book by the table is the same as 'the table holding the book up'; listing both counts the same force twice.

distractors.answer: The diagram is correct because the normal force and the table's support force are separate forces
distractors.explanation: The normal force is the contact force exerted on the book by the table; they are the same force, not two different forces.

distractors.answer: The diagram has an error: the gravitational force should not be included because the book is stationary
distractors.explanation: The gravitational force always acts on objects near Earth regardless of their state of motion; it must be included.

distractors.answer: The diagram has an error: friction should be included since the book is in contact with the table
distractors.explanation: Friction only acts when there is a tendency to slide; a book at rest on a horizontal table with no horizontal force has no friction.

toLevel5.question: Two students analyse a box being pushed at constant velocity across a rough floor. Student A states that the applied force equals friction. Student B states that the applied force is greater because the box is moving. Which one of the following best evaluates these claims?
toLevel5.correct: Student A is correct; constant velocity means zero net force, so the applied force equals friction
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Newton's first law: constant velocity means zero acceleration and zero net force, requiring the applied force to exactly balance friction.

distractors.answer: Student B is correct; motion requires the applied force to exceed all resistive forces
distractors.explanation: Motion at constant velocity does not require a net force; only acceleration requires a net force.

distractors.answer: Both are correct depending on whether kinetic or static friction is considered
distractors.explanation: At constant velocity, kinetic friction acts and must be exactly balanced by the applied force; Student B is incorrect regardless.

distractors.answer: Neither is correct; the normal force determines whether the box moves at constant velocity
distractors.explanation: The normal force acts vertically and does not directly determine horizontal motion; Student A's analysis is correct.

toLevel5.question: A ball is thrown vertically upward and reaches the top of its trajectory, where it is momentarily at rest. A second ball hangs at rest from a string. A student claims the free-body diagrams are identical because both balls are stationary. Which one of the following best evaluates this claim?
toLevel5.correct: The claim is incorrect; the thrown ball has only the gravitational force acting on it, while the hanging ball has both the gravitational force and tension
toLevel5.correctExplanation: At the top of the trajectory, only the gravitational force acts (the ball momentarily has zero velocity but still accelerates). The hanging ball has the gravitational force balanced by tension.

distractors.answer: The claim is correct because both balls are momentarily stationary at that instant
distractors.explanation: Being momentarily at rest does not mean the forces are the same; the hanging ball has tension while the thrown ball does not.

distractors.answer: The claim is incorrect because the thrown ball has zero forces at the top, since its velocity and acceleration are both zero
distractors.explanation: At the top, velocity is zero but acceleration is 9.8 m s⁻² downward due to the gravitational force; the gravitational force still acts.

distractors.answer: The claim is incorrect because the thrown ball has the gravitational force and a separate upward deceleration force
distractors.explanation: There is no 'deceleration force'; the ball decelerates because of the gravitational force alone. The hanging ball also has tension.

toLevel5.question: A student claims that on an inclined plane, the normal force and friction always add up to equal the gravitational force on the object. Which one of the following best evaluates this claim?
toLevel5.correct: The claim is incorrect; the normal force and friction are perpendicular to each other, and their vector sum equals the gravitational force
toLevel5.correctExplanation: The normal force and friction act at right angles. Their vector sum (not arithmetic sum) equals the gravitational force for an object in equilibrium on an incline.

distractors.answer: The claim is correct; forces on an incline must always balance to prevent the object from sliding
distractors.explanation: While forces balance in equilibrium, the arithmetic sum of the normal force and friction does not equal the gravitational force; their vector sum does.

distractors.answer: The claim is incorrect; only the normal force equals the gravitational force on any inclined surface
distractors.explanation: On an incline, the normal force equals mg cos θ, which is less than the gravitational force; friction provides the remaining balance.

distractors.answer: The claim is correct; this is a direct consequence of Newton's third law
distractors.explanation: Newton's third law describes action-reaction pairs between different bodies, not the force balance on a single object.

toLevel5.question: A mass of 3.0 kg is suspended from two ropes at different angles to the ceiling. Student A resolves the tensions into components to find the net upward force. Student B adds the tension magnitudes directly. Which one of the following best evaluates these approaches?
toLevel5.correct: Student A's component method is correct; the vertical components of each tension must be added separately
toLevel5.correctExplanation: When ropes are at angles, only the vertical components of tension support the gravitational force. Adding magnitudes ignores the angles and gives an incorrect result.

distractors.answer: Student B's approach is correct because tension acts entirely upward along each rope
distractors.explanation: Tension acts along each rope's direction, not purely upward; only the vertical components act upward.

distractors.answer: Both approaches give the same answer because the object is in static equilibrium
distractors.explanation: Equilibrium does not make both methods equivalent; component resolution is necessary when forces are at angles.

distractors.answer: Neither approach is correct; the angle between the two ropes must be used directly
distractors.explanation: Student A's component method is the standard and correct approach for resolving angled forces.

toLevel5.question: A skier of mass 70 kg travels downhill at constant velocity on a slope inclined at 20° to the horizontal. The free-body diagram shows the gravitational force, the normal force, and friction. Which one of the following correctly identifies the relationship between the forces?
toLevel5.correct: Friction up the slope equals mg sin 20° and the normal force equals mg cos 20°
toLevel5.correctExplanation: At constant velocity, the net force is zero. Friction balances the gravitational force component along the slope (mg sin 20°) and the normal force balances the perpendicular component (mg cos 20°).

distractors.answer: Friction up the slope equals mg cos 20° and the normal force equals mg sin 20°
distractors.explanation: This reverses the components; the component along the slope is mg sin θ and the perpendicular component is mg cos θ.

distractors.answer: Friction equals zero because the skier is moving at constant velocity
distractors.explanation: Friction is needed to balance the gravitational force component along the slope; without it the skier would accelerate.

distractors.answer: Friction up the slope equals the full gravitational force mg and the normal force is zero
distractors.explanation: On an incline, both components are less than mg; the normal force cannot be zero if the skier is in contact with the slope.

toLevel5.question: A box rests on a rough horizontal surface. A student pushes the box with a force directed downward at an angle to the horizontal. Compared to pushing horizontally, which one of the following best describes how the downward-angled push affects the free-body diagram?
toLevel5.correct: The normal force increases and friction increases because the vertical component of the push adds to the gravitational force
toLevel5.correctExplanation: A downward component of the push adds to the gravitational force on the surface, increasing the normal force. Since friction depends on the normal force, friction also increases.

distractors.answer: The normal force decreases because the angled push partially lifts the box off the surface
distractors.explanation: A push angled downward adds to the load on the surface; an upward-angled pull would reduce the normal force.

distractors.answer: The normal force remains the same because only the horizontal push component matters
distractors.explanation: The vertical component of the angled push affects the vertical force balance, changing the normal force.

distractors.answer: Friction decreases because the downward push presses the box more firmly into the surface
distractors.explanation: Pressing more firmly into the surface increases the normal force, which increases friction, not decreases it.

toLevel5.question: A student analyses two systems. System 1: a block of mass 5.0 kg on a frictionless ramp at 30° to the horizontal. System 2: an identical block on a frictionless ramp at 60° to the horizontal. Which one of the following correctly compares the free-body diagrams?
toLevel5.correct: System 2 has a larger gravitational force component along the slope and a smaller normal force than System 1
toLevel5.correctExplanation: mg sin 60° > mg sin 30° (larger along-slope component) and mg cos 60° < mg cos 30° (smaller normal force) for the steeper ramp.

distractors.answer: Both systems have identical free-body diagrams because the blocks have equal mass
distractors.explanation: Equal mass means equal gravitational force, but the resolved components differ because the angles are different.

distractors.answer: System 1 has a larger gravitational force component along the slope because shallower ramps produce more gravitational pull
distractors.explanation: mg sin 30° < mg sin 60°; steeper slopes produce larger components along the slope, not shallower ones.

distractors.answer: System 2 has a larger normal force because the steeper ramp pushes harder on the block
distractors.explanation: Normal force = mg cos θ; cos 60° < cos 30°, so the steeper ramp actually has a smaller normal force.

toLevel5.prompt: A student draws a free-body diagram of a book sliding across a table, showing the gravitational force, the normal force, and friction, but omits one force. Complete the following evaluation.
toLevel5.sentence: The student omits the {{blank:1}}. This omission means the diagram incorrectly suggests the book is {{blank:2}}.

1.correctExplanation: If the book is sliding (being pushed), the applied force causing the motion should be shown on the diagram.

distractors.answer: air resistance
distractors.explanation: For a book sliding on a table, air resistance is typically negligible; the missing force is the applied push.

distractors.answer: gravitational field
distractors.explanation: The gravitational force is already shown on the diagram; it is the applied force that is missing.

2.correctExplanation: With only friction as the horizontal force, the net force would be backward, implying the book is decelerating rather than being actively pushed.

distractors.answer: accelerating forward
distractors.explanation: Without an applied force, friction alone would cause deceleration, not forward acceleration.

distractors.answer: in equilibrium
distractors.explanation: The book is described as sliding; if friction were the only horizontal force, it would decelerate, not be in equilibrium.

toLevel5.prompt: A block of mass 10 kg sits on an incline at 45° to the horizontal. Complete the following calculation of the gravitational force components.
toLevel5.sentence: The component of the gravitational force along the slope is 10 × 9.8 × sin 45° = {{blank:1}} N. The normal force equals 10 × 9.8 × cos 45° = {{blank:2}} N.

1.correctExplanation: mg sin 45° = 98 × 0.707 = 69.3 N, which is the component of the gravitational force parallel to the slope.

distractors.explanation: 49.0 N = mg sin 30°; this uses the wrong angle. At 45°, sin 45° = 0.707, giving 69.3 N.
98.0 N is the full gravitational force; the component along the slope is mg sin 45°, which is less than the full gravitational force.

2.correctExplanation: mg cos 45° = 98 × 0.707 = 69.3 N. At 45°, sin and cos are equal, so both components have the same magnitude.

distractors.explanation: 98 N is the full gravitational force; the normal force on a 45° incline equals mg cos 45° = 69.3 N.
84.9 N = mg cos 30°; this uses the wrong angle. At 45°, the normal force is 69.3 N.
